doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: Wacky image, radio airplay and not being calculated
summary: Fleck describes the carnival side of the band and its early hope for airplay and a hit video. He says audiences like them for being different and he does not want the music to seem calculated, citing Phish.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: A successful band makes for a good name I think.
Right. The Beatles was the classic, right.

Yeah. But I mean it does sound like — you know, it’s like the Flintstones, if it’s going to be wacky, you know. And it is wacky a little bit. You know we’ve got our crazy drummer guy that plays the synth-axe with his fingers and you’ve got the banjo player playing in the jazz group and we had a harmonica player for a long time who played piano at the same time. Victor spinning the bass. There was that sort of carnival aspect to the music. But as time goes on I think we more and more want to make sure the music is soulful and meaningful to us and we’re less and less — I mean for one thing we don’t ever think about radio anymore. There was a period in the beginning where there was always that possibility that a song like “Sinister Minister” might get airplay. Or like we had a big video on that song, which did great things for the group. It got us on television, built us an audience very quickly. And then from then on the next several records there was always the possibility if we came up with a certain song that maybe that would happen again and it would go to the next level. And of course the record company really wanted to see that happen. So we sort of listened to that and think about that a little bit. But more and more we don’t get airplay and nothing like that happens and our audience has come

to like us for being different. And I remember all the things with Phish for instance. People would say, “oh go see them live, the records are sell-outs.” I don’t ever want anybody to say that about us, whether it was true or not, I never thought it was true. I thought Phish made cool records. They were fun. The records were nice. But you know what I mean? So where people mistrust you because of your motives. What are your motives? You can hear when somebody does a record and you listen to it you can tell within twenty seconds what the motives are behind recording that piece of music, whether it’s for artistic reasons or whether it’s for commercial reasons. You can tell instantly. I promise you, you can. You can tell.
And I don’t want that. I mean I don’t want that at all.
You don’t want people to think of your music as being created to —
As being calculated. Being calculated to sell records or to reach a certain audience. That’s just not what — we don’t have to do that. We’re just really fortunate that we don’t have to do that.
